hook: An excerpt from the Apollo 17 Crew Debriefing for Science (January 8, 1973), in which UV experiment co-investigator Dick Henry reports unexpected ultraviolet radiation detected at high galactic latitudes — a spectrum matching hot stars where no hot stars were visible — and discusses unresolved mysteries about the Coma cluster's gravitational binding.
why_it_matters: This document is included in the PURSUE UAP disclosure release because it shows NASA astronauts and scientists directly confronting anomalous observational data — a UV spectrum with no identifiable source — from instruments operated in space during Apollo 17. Henry explicitly states the most conservative explanation (interstellar dust reflection) does not fully account for the spectral characteristics observed, leaving open the possibility of extragalactic radiation of unknown origin. While the phenomena described are astrophysical rather than UAP in the conventional sense, the document demonstrates NASA's direct encounter with unexplained signal anomalies requiring further study.

key_findings.finding: UV radiation was detected at high galactic latitudes (North and South Galactic Poles) that matched the spectrum of hot stars, but no hot stars were present in the instrument's field of view — an anomalous result with no fully satisfying explanation.

quotes.text: The spectrum that we see looks like the spectrum of the hot
star; however, we know that there were no hot stars within our field of view.

key_findings.finding: The most conservative interpretation — that the UV signal is starlight from the galactic plane reflecting off interstellar dust — does not fully fit the observed spectral characteristics, and extragalactic radiation remains a possible explanation.

quotes.text: Therefore, the most conservative interpretation, I think, is that what we're seeing is light from hot stars in the galactic plane going up out of the plane and reflecting off interstellar dust. There are certain characteristics of the spectrum, though, that don't fit that theory, and it's at least possible that this is extragalactic radiation.

key_findings.finding: The Apollo 17 UV experiment successfully detected a signal above the instrument's dark count, meaning the high dark current anomaly did not compromise this particular result.

quotes.text: The spectrum that we see is above this dark count. In other words, this abnormally high dark current did not, in fact, interfere with that experiment.

key_findings.finding: Henry reports that ionized hydrogen searches in the Coma cluster failed — Lyman-alpha radiation was not detected, ruling out ionized hydrogen as the gravitational binding agent and leaving an unresolved mystery about what holds the cluster together.

quotes.text: We looked for Lyman-alpha radiation, red shifted from the ionized hydrogen, and we didn't see any. We set a lower limit, which certainly excludes the possibility that the Coma cluster is held together by this ionized hydrogen. I think that may leave a real mystery as to what is holding the thing together.

key_findings.finding: Apollo 17 acquired a large volume of Lyman-alpha hydrogen data about interstellar hydrogen streaming through the solar system, data expected to significantly advance understanding of this phenomenon — full analysis was pending detailed computer study.

quotes.text: We obtained Just an enormous amount of data on the Apollo that's going to straighten out this picture and clarify it considerably. This is hydrogen that is inside our solar system. It's sunlight reflecting off this. The hydrogen, Gary Thomas thinks, is hydrogen from interstellar space streaming through the solar system, and he is looking forward with great anticipation to getting detailed analyses of that.

legacy_program_connections.reasoning: The document's inclusion in the PURSUE UAP disclosure release suggests it was reviewed for relevance to anomalous phenomena detection, though its content is astrophysical rather than UAP-investigative in the conventional sense.
